name: Mastercam
tagline: CAD/CAM software that turns part models into verified toolpaths and machine-ready G-code for mills, lathes, routers, and wire EDM.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Sold through resellers as a perpetual or subscription license with annual maintenance, quoted per module and per machine type, typically in the thousands.

verdictSummary: You can absolutely get an agent to write a G-code generator in an afternoon: parse a profile, offset it, ramp down in passes, spit out G1 moves. What you cannot one-shot is the part that matters, which is the post processor for your specific control, gouge and collision checking, stock-aware roughing on real 3D surfaces, feeds and speeds that do not snap a tool, and the backplot you trust enough to press cycle start. Mastercam's actual product is thousands of validated machine posts plus decades of toolpath edge cases found by other people's broken endmills. A wrong line of G-code is not a bug report, it is a scrapped part, a wrecked fixture, or a spindle crash. The consolation build is real and useful for 2.5D work on a hobby router; it is not a replacement for a production shop.
coreLoopDIY: Takes an SVG or DXF outline plus a few parameters and emits 2.5D contour and pocket G-code with an on-screen backplot, for a single known machine dialect.
requirements: Python 3.11 and a local machine, no server needed
Flat 2D geometry exported as SVG or DXF, no solids
A machine whose G-code dialect you already know by hand (GRBL or LinuxCNC)
A tool and feeds table you supply yourself
Willingness to air-cut every program before touching stock
whatYouLose: Post processors: Mastercam ships validated posts for thousands of control and kinematic combinations, you get one dialect you hardcoded
3D surfacing, multiaxis, lathe, mill-turn, and wire EDM strategies, all of which are years of work each
Stock-aware roughing, rest machining, gouge checking, and holder collision detection
Verified simulation, so your only verification is a wireframe backplot and your own nerves
Any support path when a part fails, plus the hiring pool of machinists who already know the software
moatNotes: The post processor library is the unglamorous asset. It is also why shops that already run Mastercam keep running Mastercam: the posts are tuned, the macros are written, and the operators are trained.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the software is cheap compared to the machine it drives, the stock it cuts, and the hour of downtime it avoids. A mid-size shop with a 150k machining center and a backlog is not shopping for a toolpath hobby project, it is buying a known-good chain from model to spindle, with a reseller to call when the post emits something strange. The licensing is annoying and the UI is a museum of software history, but the output is trusted, and trust is the entire purchase.
notes: Toolpath math is a weekend; trusting it with a 10,000 RPM spindle is not. The moat is the validated post processor library for thousands of machine and control combinations, plus every crash someone else already paid for.
prompt:
Build a local 2.5D CAM utility in Python 3.11 called pocketcam. Single CLI tool, no server, no accounts, no telemetry, no cloud.

Scope, in:
- Input: a single SVG or DXF file containing closed 2D polylines and circles, units in mm.
- Geometry: flatten beziers and arcs to polylines at a configurable tolerance, detect closed loops, detect which loops are holes via even-odd containment.
- Toolpaths: contour (inside, outside, on-line) with cutter compensation applied in software, and pocket clearing via offset-inward passes with a configurable stepover.
- Depth: multiple Z passes to a target depth with a configurable stepdown, plus a plunge mode of straight, ramp, or helix for pockets.
- Output: GRBL-flavored G-code only. G21, G90, absolute arcs off, G1 linear moves only, no canned cycles. Header and footer configurable in the job file.
- Job definition: a YAML file holding tool diameter, feed, plunge feed, spindle RPM, stepover, stepdown, safe Z, target depth, and per-loop operation assignment.
- Backplot: render the toolpath to an SVG and to a matplotlib window, color rapids red and cutting moves blue, so the operator can eyeball it before running.
- Safety checks: refuse to emit if tool radius exceeds the narrowest offsetable width of a pocket, if plunge feed is zero, or if any cut move sits above safe Z.
- Tests: pytest covering offsetting, hole detection, and that no emitted rapid ever occurs below safe Z.

Scope, out, and say so in the README:
- No 3D surfacing, no multiaxis, no lathe, no mill-turn.
- No collision or holder checking, no stock model, no rest machining.
- No post processors beyond GRBL. Anything else is the user's job.
- No feeds and speeds calculator. The job file is the source of truth.

Stack: Python 3.11, shapely for offsetting, ezdxf for DXF, svgpathtools for SVG, click for the CLI, pyyaml, matplotlib for the plot, pytest. Use uv for dependency management. No .env needed since there are no secrets.

Deliver: src layout, a working example job and SVG in examples/, a README that opens with a blunt warning to air-cut every program above the stock before cutting anything, and a one-command demo that writes out.nc plus backplot.svg.
